lesson_title: Two Piles, One Answer: Resultants by the Component Method
hook_text: Walk 90 metres east, 120 metres north. Your legs did 210 metres — but you are only 150 metres from home. That gap is the whole topic.
clip_script: Walk 90 metres east, then 120 metres north. Your legs did 210 metres of pavement. But a hadeda flying straight from your gate to you covers only 150. That straight flight is the RESULTANT — the one trip that does the work of the whole zigzag. Now the part everyone fears, and it should fear you instead. Someone drags a hockey bag with the strap sloping up. That pull is doing two jobs at once: dragging forward AND lifting. So sort it, like a tuck-shop owner sorting coins into piles. One pile forward, one pile up. A 300 newton pull at 40 degrees gives 229,8 newtons forward and 192,8 newtons up. Do that to every force. Add the sideways pile — west wears a minus. Add the upward pile — south wears a minus. Two arrows at right angles, and that is the hadeda problem again. Square, add, root: 284,2 newtons. Divide up by sideways, press inverse tangent: 73,7 degrees. Split, add, rebuild. Three moves. And never hand in a size without its direction.
visual_style: A suburban street grid from above, a walking route lighting up leg by leg with the diagonal snapping into place; then a sloped bag strap splitting into two glowing arrows; finally four tangled arrows collapsing into two, then one.
mood: Brisk and reassuring — an intimidating topic quietly turning into coin-sorting.
pacing: Fast opening reveal, steady beat through the sorting, punchy three-word finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn any four forces into one clean answer.
